docs.title: pyMachDM: Machine Learning-Based Decision-Makers in Python
🏷️ About
docs.text:
pyMachDM is an open-source Python package that benchmarks interactive multi-criteria decision-making (iMCDM) methods by simulating human preferences using machine learning-based decision makers (Machine-DM).

pip install pyMachDM

docs.title: ⚠️ Disclaimer
docs.text:
We acknowledge that:

  • Human decision-making cannot be fully replicated by Machine-DM
  • The primary goal is to enable systematic benchmarking of iMCDM methods
  • The framework provides a digital platform for interactive MCDM research and development
  • We hope to facilitate the design of more effective iMCDM methods for real-world use

        K = 5

        g = 1 + 9/4 * (x[1] + x[2] + x[3] + x[4])

class STEM_Problem(ElementwiseProblem):
    def __init__(self, problem=None, start_F=None, eps=None, i1=None, i2=None, i3=None, i4=None, mode=None,
                 ideal_point=None, nadir_point=None):

        self.problem = problem
        self.start_F = np.array(start_F)
        self.eps = eps

        self.i1 = np.array(i1) if i1 is not None else np.array([])
        self.i2 = np.array(i2) if i2 is not None else np.array([])
        self.i3 = np.array(i3) if i3 is not None else np.array([])
        self.i4 = np.array(i4) if i4 is not None else np.array([])
        self.mode = mode
        self.n_ieq = len(self.i1) + len(self.i2) + len(self.i3) + len(self.i4)

        self.ideal_point = np.array(ideal_point)
        self.nadir_point = np.array(nadir_point)
        self.rho = 0.001
#         print("Ideal, Nadir:", ideal_point, nadir_point)
        # Count constraints from the base problem
        n_ieq_constr_base = getattr(problem, "n_ieq_constr", 0)
        n_eq_constr_base = getattr(problem, "n_eq_constr", 0)

        # For STEM 'sub' mode, include additional constraints
        n_ieq_constr_total = (self.n_ieq if mode == 'sub' else 0) + n_ieq_constr_base
        n_eq_constr_total = n_eq_constr_base

        super().__init__(
            n_var=self.problem.n_var,
            n_obj=1,
            n_ieq_constr=n_ieq_constr_total,
            n_eq_constr=n_eq_constr_total,
            xl=self.problem.xl,
            xu=self.problem.xu
        )

    def _evaluate(self, x, out, *args, **kwargs):
        # Evaluate original problem
        base_out = {}
        self.problem._evaluate(x, base_out)

        f = np.array(base_out.get("F"))
        G_base = np.array(base_out.get("G", []))  # inequality constraints (<=0)
        H_base = np.array(base_out.get("H", []))  # equality constraints (=0)

        # Handle empty constraints gracefully
        if G_base.size == 0:
            G_base = np.empty(0)
        if H_base.size == 0:
            H_base = np.empty(0)

        # Combined index set
        if len(self.i1) == 0 and len(self.i2) == 0 and len(self.i3) == 0 and len(self.i4) == 0:
            i1234 = np.arange(len(f))
        else:
            i1234 = np.concatenate([self.i1, self.i2, self.i3, self.i4])

        # --- Start mode ---
        if self.mode == 'start':

            F = np.max((f[i1234]-self.start_F[i1234])/(self.nadir_point[i1234]-self.ideal_point[i1234]) + 
                   self.rho*np.sum((f[i1234])/(self.nadir_point[i1234]-self.ideal_point[i1234])))
            
            out["F"] = [F]
            out["G"] = G_base
            out["H"] = H_base

        # --- Subproblem mode ---
        elif self.mode == 'sub':
        
            e = (self.nadir_point - self.ideal_point)/(self.nadir_point*(self.ideal_point+0.001))
            w = e/np.sum(e)
            w[self.i4] = 0 
            w[self.i3] = 0

            if len(self.i1) == 0 and len(self.i2) == 0:
                G1 = []  # nothing to compute
            else:
                i12 = np.concatenate([self.i1, self.i2])
                i12 = [i for i in i12 if i < len(f)]
                G1 = [f[i] - self.start_F[i] for i in i12]

            G2 = [f[j] - self.start_F[j] for j in self.i3]
            G3 = [f[k] - self.eps[k] for k in self.i4]

            F = np.max(abs(w[i1234]*(f[i1234]-self.ideal_point[i1234])))
#             print(G1,G2,G3)

            G_step = np.concatenate([G1, G2, G3])

            # Combine with original problem constraints
            out["F"] = [F]
            out["G"] = np.concatenate([G_base, G_step]) if G_base.size > 0 else G_step
            out["H"] = H_base

        else:
            raise ValueError("mode must be 'start', or 'sub'")

docs.title: Multi-objective Optimization
docs.text:
• Core Concept: Optimization of multiple, mutually conflicting objective functions simultaneously where no single optimal solution exists.
  • Goal: To identify the "Pareto optimal" set—solutions where one objective cannot be improved without degrading another.

docs.title: ⚙️ Formulation
docs.text:
\[ \begin{aligned} \text{minimize} \quad & \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x}) = \left\{ f_1(\mathbf{x}), f_2(\mathbf{x}), \dots, f_M(\mathbf{x}) \right\}^T \\ \text{subject to} \quad & g_j(\mathbf{x}) \le 0, \quad j = 1, 2, \dots, J \\ & h_k(\mathbf{x}) = 0, \quad k = 1, 2, \dots, K \\ & x_i^{LB} \leq x_i \leq x_i^{UB}, \quad i = 1, 2, \dots, n. \end{aligned} \]

where-

  • \(\mathbf{x}\): The \(n\)-dimensional decision variable vector within the feasible space \(\mathcal{S}\).
  • \(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})\): The objective vector representing \(m\) distinct criteria (\(m \ge 2\)).
  • \(g_j(\mathbf{x})\): \(J\) inequality constraints.
  • \(h_k(\mathbf{x})\): \(K\) equality constraints.

docs.title: ⚖️ MCDM Methods
docs.text:
• A Priori Methods: Preferences, goals, or hard constraints are explicitly specified by the user before running the optimization routine.
  • A Posteriori Methods: The algorithm generates a wide array of Pareto-optimal trade-offs first; the user selects the final operating design afterward.
  • Interactive Methods: A tight, real-time loop where the system generates candidate options, the user gives feedback, and the algorithm continuously adapts its search path.

docs.title: 📊 Visualization
docs.text:
• Core Purpose: Serves as the interactive cognitive interface enabling users to interpret complex, high-dimensional trade-off spaces.
  • Parallel Coordinates Plots: Maps highly dimensional parameters along vertical parallel axes, allowing real-time filtering of solution pathways.
  • Scatter Plot Matrices (Brushing & Linking): Linking interactive charts so selecting data points on an objective trade-off front highlights its physical decision variables everywhere else instantly.

docs.title: Weighted-sum
docs.text:
• Mathematical Formulation:

\(U(\mathbf{x}) = \sum\limits_{i=1}^{M} w_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\)

  • Description: Condenses multi-dimensional objectives into a single scalar score by multiplying each objective by an assigned weight (\(w_i\)). It is simple to compute but completely fails to identify or reach optimal solutions located in non-convex regions of the Pareto front.

docs.title: Tchebycheff
docs.text:
• Mathematical Formulation:

\(\text{minimize} \quad \max\limits_{i=1 \dots M} \left[ \dfrac{| f_i(\mathbf{x}) - z_i^* |}{w_i} \right]\)

  • Description: Minimizes the maximum weighted distance between a solution and a theoretical ideal reference point (\(\mathbf{z}^*\)). While it can find solutions along any non-convex Pareto shape, its strict geometric boundaries can occasionally yield weakly Pareto-optimal points.

docs.title: ASF
docs.text:
• Mathematical Formulation:

\(\text{minimize} \quad \max\limits_{i=1 \dots M} \left[ \dfrac{f_i(\mathbf{x}) - \hat{z}_i}{z_i^{\rm nad}-z_i^{**}} \right]\)

  • Description: A flexible variation of the Tchebycheff metric that replaces the absolute ideal bounds with an arbitrary, user-defined aspiration target (\(\mathbf{\hat{z}}\)). If the target is unfeasible, it finds the closest available alternative; if the target is easily reached, it continues to optimize past it.

docs.title: AASF
docs.text:
• Mathematical Formulation:

\(\text{minimize} \quad \max\limits_{i=1 \dots M} \left[ \dfrac{f_i(\mathbf{x}) - \hat{z}_i}{z_i^{\rm nad}-z_i^{**}} \right]+ \rho \sum\limits_{i=1}^{M} \left[ \dfrac{f_i(\mathbf{x})}{z_i^{\rm nad}-z_i^{**}} \right]\)

  • Description: Introduces a linear weighted sum regularization term to the primary ASF framework, scaled by a small positive augmentation parameter (\(\rho > 0\)). This addition mathematical eliminates edge anomalies, ensuring all generated trade-offs are strictly Pareto-optimal.

docs.title: Intra-objective Class Comparison
docs.text: \(\max \big(\bar{z}_i^n, \varepsilon_j^n \big),\ \forall i \in \textbf{I}^{\leq}, \forall j \in \textbf{I}^{\geq}\)

docs.title: \(\mathcal{M}_{PE}\) Metric
docs.text:
\(\mathcal{M}_{PE} = \max_{m=1}^{M} (3-I_m) + \left\{\max \big(\bar{z}_i^n, \varepsilon_j^n \big),\ \forall i \in \textbf{I}^{\leq}, \forall j \in \textbf{I}^{\geq}\right\}\)

The values of \(\bar{z}_i^n\) and \(\varepsilon_j^n\) are obtained by normalizing the bounding parameters \(\varepsilon_j\) and \(\bar{z}_i\) between 0 and 1, with respect to the target point \(\mathbf{f}^T\), as follows:

\(\bar{z}_i^n = \dfrac{\bar{z}_i - f_i^T}{f_i^R - f_i^T}\), \(\varepsilon_j^n = \dfrac{f_j^T - \varepsilon_j}{f_j^T - f_j^{\ast}}\)
